newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Soyinka denies involved in Nigerian bomb blasts.
newsitem.headline: Soyinka denies involved in Nigerian bomb blasts.

text.p: Exiled Nigerian opposition leader and Nobel prize winner for literature Wole Soyinka on Friday denied any involvement in Lagos bomb blasts that wounded 16 soldiers but refused to condemn the action.

"I cannot condemn violence directed at (General Sani) Abacha's regime," he told British Broadcasting Corporation radio in London, adding "I approve of action that is necessary to terminate the existence of the Abacha regime so does any organisation to which I belong."
Asked who was responsible for the explosions, he said: "I do not know. I am not in Nigeria."
Two bomb explosions in Lagos this week aimed at Abacha's close ally and military administrator of Lagos state Colonel Muhammed Marwa wounded 16 soldiers and three civilians.
Many Nigerians have condemned the attacks and on Thursday a large group staged a rally in solidarity with Marwa in Lagos.
So far no one has claimed responsibility but police have said the recent wave of bomb blasts was the handiwork of the exiled opposition.

According to the police, victims of a bungled car bomb explosion in Lagos in November were agents of Soyinka, who leads the National Liberation Council of Nigeria (NALICON) based abroad and which has vowed to topple Abacha.
"This whole scream about Wole Soyinka is simply part of a plot to set us up for murder, to be able to say those who live by the sword shall die by the sword," Soyinka said.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, has been in turmoil since June 1993 when the-then army ruler annulled a presidential election that would have restored democracy.

Soyinka is fighting for the annulment to be reversed and Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the vote who has been detained since he proclaimed himself president in 1994, to be freed and installed president.

But Abacha, who seized power in the chaos of 1993 is pursuing his own programme to hand over to a democratically elected president in 1998 although his critics say his "hidden agenda" is to hang on to power.
